title: Quantifier Inference Rules and their Side Conditions
quickIdea: Four rules move quantifiers in and out of a proof. The side conditions - arbitrary name versus fresh name - are where the marks are lost.
remember: Universal instantiation: from for all x P(x) infer P(c) for any name c that denotes an element of the domain.
Universal generalisation: from P(c) for an arbitrary c infer for all x P(x). The name must be arbitrary, not one introduced by an existential assumption.
Existential instantiation: from there exists x P(x) infer P(c) for a fresh name c that has not been used before.
Existential generalisation: from P(c) infer there exists x P(x).
You may not generalise over a name introduced by existential instantiation, and you may not instantiate a universal with a name outside the domain.
Apply existential instantiation before universal instantiation when both are needed, so the fresh name stays fresh.
These rules justify each step of the falsification and derivation arguments used elsewhere; they are the proof-theoretic counterpart of the semantic validity tests.

example.prompt: From for all x (P(x) implies Q(x)) and there exists x P(x), derive there exists x Q(x).
example.work: Existential instantiation gives P(c) with c fresh. Universal instantiation on the first premise gives P(c) implies Q(c). Modus ponens gives Q(c). Existential generalisation gives there exists x Q(x).
example.answer: There exists x Q(x), derived with a name that is fresh and then discharged.

gateAngle: No verified PYQ in this repository turns on a named inference rule; the rules matter because they justify every step of the validity arguments the other first-order cards use, and a wrong option in a validity question is usually a step that breaks one of the side conditions.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: From there exists x P(x), may you infer for all x P(x)?
variations.why: The witness is one element. Universal generalisation needs a name that was arbitrary, and an existential witness is not arbitrary.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: From for all x (P(x) implies Q(x)) and not Q(c), what follows about P(c)?
variations.answer: Not P(c), by universal instantiation and modus tollens.
variations.why: Instantiating the universal at c gives P(c) implies Q(c); with not Q(c), modus tollens yields not P(c).

trap.why: The witness was chosen to satisfy P; it is not an arbitrary element, so what holds for it need not hold for the whole domain.
trap.counterexample: Domain the integers, P(x): x is prime. There exists x P(x) is true and P(2) is true, but for all x P(x) is false.

check.question: Why must the name introduced by existential instantiation be fresh?
check.answer: Because the witness is an arbitrary element known only to satisfy the predicate; reusing an existing name would import facts already known about that element.
check.explanation: Freshness keeps the assumption tied to the existential alone, so the conclusion does not depend on anything else known about the named object.
